slides.lectureTitle: Introducing the Hardware for the Robot
slides.title: Structural Materials — Trade-offs for Robot Design

visualInspection.notes: Full six-row materials table inspected: steel 5 stars/heavy/low cost/industrial welding; aluminum 4 stars/light/medium/cobots and drones; CFRP 5 stars/very light/high/medical and aerospace; titanium 5 stars/medium/very high/surgical; engineering plastics 2 stars/very light/very low/education; soft silicone flexible/light/medium/soft grippers and wearables. Qualitative class-level tradeoffs, not universal grade-specific strength rankings. Lighter links reduce inertia under comparable geometry, but faster tracking and easier learning are not unconditional guarantees. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.lectureTitle: Introducing the Hardware for the Robot
slides.title: Actuators :

visualInspection.notes: Hydraulic and pneumatic descriptions plus both cutaway cylinders viewed. Hydraulic upper image has rod extending left, right-port inward arrow and left-port outward arrow; pneumatic lower image has rod right, left-port inward blue arrow and right-port outward green arrow. Hydraulic high force and actuator-level power density are balanced against peripheral pump/plumbing mass, leaks and seal friction. Air compressibility and seal friction complicate pneumatic control. Cleaner refers to working-fluid leakage, not a guarantee of zero exhaust contamination. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.lectureTitle: Introducing the Hardware for the Robot
slides.title: Electric Motors :

visualInspection.notes: Brushed DC text: stationary brushes contact revolving commutator to energize rotor windings; torque proportional to winding current in the stated model; winding overheating limits sustained operation. Electric motors are controllable and easy to interface. The unlabelled cutaway is generic motor imagery and is not proof of a visible brushed commutator. Relative fluid-versus-electric power density depends on the comparison boundary. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.lectureTitle: Introducing the Hardware for the Robot
slides.title: Electric Motors :

visualInspection.notes: Brushless: stationary windings and rotating magnetic rotor, electronic commutation from shaft position, reduced brush wear and favorable cooling. Internal shaft sensor is an example, not mandatory because sensorless commutation exists. Claims of infrequent AC motors and low-torque steppers need historical/task qualification, not current blanket truth. Better cooling and torque are design-dependent. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.lectureTitle: Introducing the Hardware for the Robot
slides.title: End-Effectors & Grippers — How Robots Touch the World

visualInspection.notes: Five gripper boxes inspected: two-finger parallel for boxes/warehouse; three-finger adaptive for irregular shapes; vacuum for flat packages/glass; inflatable silicone soft fingers for delicate food/medical; magnetic for metal sheets/castings. Magnetic attraction needs suitable material, not all metals. Vacuum needs an appropriate seal/surface and payload margin. End-effector is terminal tool/device, not necessarily the structural last link itself. Simpler action space can ease learning but does not guarantee task success. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.lectureTitle: Introducing the Hardware for the Robot
slides.title: Sensor Classification — Proprioceptive vs. Exteroceptive

visualInspection.notes: Two-column sensor classification: source places encoders, IMU, current sensors and force/torque under proprioception; RGB, depth/LiDAR, ultrasonic and tactile arrays under exteroception. F/T contact measurements can describe external interaction, so classification is context-dependent; preserve source table without asserting a universal placement. Current is a torque estimate via a motor model, not direct contact wrench. Tactile arrays give spatial contact distribution. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: • GPU Compute Board: e.g. Jetson AGX Orin

visualInspection.notes: AGX Orin source example 2048 CUDA cores, 64 GB, 275 TOPS, 15–60 W; FPGA Zynq parallel hardware logic, deterministic, 5–20 W; cloud/5G offload for LLM planning/heavy training. slides.lectureTitle: Introducing the Hardware for the Robot
slides.title: Power Systems — Batteries, BMS & Power Distribution

visualInspection.notes: Full battery table inspected: Li-Po 150–250 Wh/kg, up to 100C, 300–500 cycles, drones/racing; Li-ion 18650 100–200 Wh/kg, 1–3C, 500–1000 cycles, mobile/humanoids; NiMH 60–120 Wh/kg, 5–10C, 500 cycles, older education; lead-acid 30–50 Wh/kg, low discharge, 200–300 cycles, heavy AGVs. Values are broad illustrative entries, not battery-selection limits. Li-Po is a lithium-ion family/package distinction and 18650 is a cylindrical form factor, not the full chemistry. All-hardware-electrical wording omits hydraulic/pneumatic mechanical power paths. BMS is in heading only, with no actual functional block diagram. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.lectureTitle: Introducing the Hardware for the Robot
slides.title: Mapping Robot Hardware to AI Concepts

visualInspection.notes: All six hardware-to-AI rows inspected. State q=[0.3,−0.1,1.2] rad; action PWM 75% claimed to yield 75% speed; reward +10 for stable grasp force; policy inference 8 ms; encoder ±0.088° claimed to map to Gaussian sigma=0.001 rad; RL step 100 Hz claimed to require IMU at least 200 Hz. Qualifications: observation need not equal full state, reward is designed from measured conditions, duty is not a universal speed percentage, a quantization bound does not determine Gaussian distribution/sigma, and Nyquist concerns signal bandwidth rather than twice a policy update rate. Better sensors can help, but performance also depends on calibration, timing, compute and algorithms. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.lectureTitle: Introducing the Hardware for the Robot
slides.title: Fusion Methods:Sensor Fusion for Robot Manipulators

visualInspection.notes: Manipulator fusion motivations: redundancy, accuracy, robustness, completeness. Sensors: encoders/resolvers joint angles/velocities; F/T end-effector six-component wrench; IMUs vibration/orientation estimates; RGB-D/stereo object and pose; tactile/skin contact distribution/slip. Methods list Kalman, EKF, particle, deep CNN/LSTM fusion and Bayesian estimation. A wrench has three force and three moment components, not six independently actuated DOFs. Fusion improvements require error models, calibration, synchronization, correlation handling and fault detection, not blind averaging. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.lectureTitle: Introducing the Hardware for the Robot
slides.title: Sensor Fusion for Mobile Robots

visualInspection.notes: Mobile palette: planar/3-D LiDAR, wheel-odometry dead reckoning, IMU, outdoor GNSS, stereo/RGB-D, near-range ultrasound/IR. Right-hand five-stage SLAM pipeline: raw LiDAR/odometry/IMU; filtering/calibration/sync; point clouds/keypoints/edges; EKF or graph-SLAM state estimation/loop closure; map and pose for planning. Not all LiDAR has 360-degree field of view. Loop closure and global consistency are algorithm/data-association goals, not guaranteed by any sensor list or EKF name. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.
